14.1–14.2 Level Curves, Limits and Continuity

14.1 finishes with graphs in Desmos, level curves and contour maps; then 14.2 defines the limit of a function of two variables, shows how two paths can prove a limit does not exist, and ends with the limit laws, the Squeeze Theorem and continuity.

2Level curves and contour maps

Slice the graph with horizontal planes and drop the slices into the xy-plane.

Board heading: Level Curves and Contour Maps

Definition

The level curves of a function are the curves , where is a fixed constant.

Under the definition he drew the graph cut by horizontal planes , and beside it a set of circles in the plane with “” under them, labelled and . Below the 3-D sketch: two small vertical planes, with “, ” written next to them (last day’s vertical traces, for contrast).

Explanation (added)

A level curve is a horizontal trace pushed straight down: points of the xy-plane where the surface has height exactly . A contour map is a picture of several level curves, usually for equally spaced . The topographic map is the everyday version: each contour is one elevation, and where contours crowd together the hill is steep. Stewart §14.1 uses this same picture to introduce level curves.

Explanation (added)

The same expression means three different things here. As an equation in , is a cylinder (any works). As a function, is a paraboloid. Its level curves are circles of radius for , the single point for , and nothing for .

For equal steps in the circles get closer together as you move out (radii ), because the paraboloid gets steeper. The cone in the second pasted note has evenly spaced circles because its slope never changes.

514.2 Limits and Continuity

Board heading: 14.2. Limits & Continuity

Underneath, a sketch of the point with moving toward it, and

Typed note included in the PDF

The big difference from Calc I

In Calc I you could approach from only two directions, left and right. In the plane, can sneak up on along infinitely many paths: lines, parabolas, spirals.

Explanation (added)

“Sufficiently close” means inside a small disk around , not just on one line through it. That is why the limit is so much harder to have in two variables: has to settle toward from every direction and along every curve at once.

7Two paths, two limits: the limit does not exist

Theorem (two-path test)

If as along a curve and as along curve , and , then

does not exist.

Explanation (added)

If the limit were , every path would have to give (the definition talks about a whole disk, and every path runs through it). So two paths with different answers rule the limit out. The test only ever proves non-existence: getting the same value along many paths proves nothing, as the example in §10 shows. The usual paths to try: the axes and , lines , and curves like .

13Continuity

Definition

A function is continuous at if

is continuous on a region of if is continuous at every point in .

Result

All polynomials and rational functions are continuous on their domains.

Example

Where is continuous?

– everywhere except at .

Explanation (added)

The definition hides three requirements: is defined, the limit exists, and the two are equal. The example is a rational function whose bottom is 0 only at the origin, so its domain is everything except , and it is continuous there by the result above. At it fails the first requirement. The limit there does exist (it is 0, §12), so defining would make it continuous everywhere.

What a typical exam question looks like
  • Sketch the level curves of a given (like or ) for a list of values: solve , name each curve, label it with its .
  • Match a contour map to a surface, or say where the surface is steep from how close the level curves are.
  • Show that a limit at does not exist by finding two paths with different values: axes first, then or , then a curve like when all the lines agree.
  • Evaluate a limit of a polynomial or rational function by direct substitution, checking the denominator is not 0.
  • Prove a limit is 0 with the Squeeze Theorem: bound by something like using .
  • Say where a function such as is continuous, with a reason.
